neighbors.heading: prayer before the day
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: come in the early hours, and bring attention, not payment. Jews know that hour. A psalm says: "O LORD, in the morning shalt Thou hear my voice; in the morning will I order my prayer unto Thee, and will look forward." Jews pray Shacharit, the morning prayer, and the rabbis trace it to Abraham, who rose early to stand before God.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the amrit vela is for remembering the Name, and the pauri says grace opens the door. For Jews, morning prayer is a commandment with set words, one of three daily prayers, said facing Jerusalem.
neighbors.shared: the first quiet of the day belongs to something bigger.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 5:4 (JPS 1917; 5:3 in many Bibles) · Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 26b (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a dawn in me
neighbors.text: Today the Japji pointed to the quiet before dawn. Henry David Thoreau, living alone by Walden Pond, felt its pull too. He called every morning a cheerful invitation, and wrote: "Morning is when I am awake and there is a dawn in me." For him the clock mattered less than the waking: being awake on the inside.
neighbors.difference: The amrit vela turns toward the One and the Name, and the door is opened by grace. Thoreau looks to nature and his own wakefulness; he names no Guru and asks for no grace.
neighbors.shared: the quiet before the day has something to give you.
neighbors.sources: Henry David Thoreau, Walden (1854), "Where I Lived, and What I Lived For"

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 8, meaning: the power of listening

neighbors.heading: we hear, and we obey
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: by listening, pain and wrongdoing are wiped away, and next comes mannai, trusting. The Qur'an pairs two steps too. Believers say: "We hear, and we obey." And it praises those "who hear advice and follow the best thereof." In Islam, the word is meant to be heard: the Qur'an is recited aloud.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the listening is to the Name and the Guru's word, and it leads to trust. In Islam, the word heard is the Qur'an, Allah's own speech, and hearing leads to following its commands.
neighbors.shared: a life changes first through the ears, then through the heart.

neighbors.heading: hear, then reflect
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said listening changes everything, and trusting comes next. The Upanishads give a ladder too. The sage Yajnavalkya tells his wife: "Verily, the Self is to be seen, to be heard, to be perceived, to be marked, O Maitreyi!" Later teachers named the steps: shravana, hearing the teaching; manana, reflecting on it; nididhyasana, meditating until it's lived.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the listening is to the Name and Gurbani, and it opens by the Guru's grace. In this Upanishad, what's heard is teaching about the Self, the atman, to be known directly by the seeker.
neighbors.shared: first you listen, then you let it change you.
neighbors.sources: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.5 (Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East) · the steps of shravana, manana, nididhyasana in Vedanta teaching (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a raft, not the shore
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said no paper, pen or writer can hold the state of the one who trusts; the scripture points past itself. The Buddha said something close about his own teaching. He compared it to a raft: built for crossing a river, not for carrying on your head once you're across. The teaching is for crossing over, not for clinging to.
neighbors.difference: The Japji says the state of trust is known only by the one who trusts the Name. The Buddha speaks of no Name and no Creator; the raft carries you to nibbana, freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the words are a way in, and the rest is lived.
neighbors.sources: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta, the simile of the raft (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: past all understanding
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said the state of the one who trusts can't be told; you only know it from inside, like water. Paul writes something close to the church at Philippi: "And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus." A peace you can't explain, only be kept by.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, that untellable state comes through trusting the Name. For Paul, the peace is God's gift through Christ Jesus, at the center of Christian faith; it keeps the heart rather than being reached by it.
neighbors.shared: some peace is too big for words, and still you can live in it.

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind

neighbors.heading: whiter than snow
neighbors.text: Today the Japji climbed a ladder: water washes the body, soap the clothes, and the love of the Name washes the mind. Catholics pray the same picture in Psalm 50, the Miserere: "Wash me yet more from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin." And: "thou shalt wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow."
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the mind is dyed in the color of the Name, and you still eat what you sow. Catholics believe sin is washed by God's mercy through Christ, given in baptism and in confession, through a priest's absolution.
neighbors.shared: a stained heart doesn't have to stay stained.

neighbors.heading: you sow, you eat
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: you yourself sow, and you yourself eat. The psychologist William James said it about habit: "We are spinning our own fates, good or evil, and never to be undone." Every small act, he wrote, leaves its little mark, so the person you'll become is built from what you do today, again and again.
neighbors.difference: The Japji sets this beside grace: the Name can dye even a stained mind clean, and all moves by the Hukam. James describes how habit works in body and brain; he promises no washing from outside.
neighbors.shared: small seeds, planted daily, become the life you live in.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890), ch. 4, "Habit"

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 24, meaning: no end to praise

neighbors.heading: mouths full of song
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: the more is said, the more there is, and praise never reaches the end. A psalm says: "Great is the LORD, and highly to be praised; and His greatness is unsearchable." And the Shabbat morning prayer Nishmat says that even if our mouths were full of song like the sea, we could never thank God enough.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs sing of the endless One in the Guru's hymns, and the pauri rests in grace, nadar. Jews praise the God of Israel in psalms and set prayers, and Nishmat thanks God for rescuing and sustaining His people.
neighbors.shared: there's always more to be thankful for than words can hold.

neighbors.heading: no end of glories
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said there's no end to the praises and no end to the One praised. In the Gita, Arjuna asks Krishna to name his glories. Krishna names many: the sun among lights, the Ganges among rivers. Then he stops. There is no end to them, he says; what he has told is only a small sample.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, Krishna, God come as a person, describes his own glories to a friend. For Sikhs, the One is never born in a body, and the Gurus praise the Formless, who alone knows His greatness.
neighbors.shared: wherever you look, there's more wonder than you can count.

neighbors.heading: put on kindness
neighbors.text: Today the Japji turned a yogi's outfit inward: contentment for earrings, meditation for ashes, faith for a staff. Paul dresses Christians the same way: "Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering." And above all these, he says, put on charity, love.
neighbors.difference: In the Japji, the inner outfit answers the yogis, and the mind is the field to win. For Paul, these virtues are the clothes of a new life in Christ, worn because "even as Christ forgave you, so also do ye."
neighbors.shared: the best thing you wear is how you treat people.

neighbors.heading: the best clothing
neighbors.text: Today the Japji traded a yogi's earrings and ashes for contentment and meditation. The Qur'an makes a similar turn: "O Children of Adam! We have revealed unto you raiment to conceal your shame, and splendid vesture, but the raiment of restraint from evil, that is best." Clothes are a gift. Goodness is the garment that counts most.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak speaks to yogis about their own gear, and calls all humanity the true order. The Qur'an speaks to all the children of Adam, and its best garment is taqwa, mindful awe of Allah.
neighbors.shared: the clothes no one can see are the ones people remember.

neighbors.heading: not by bread alone
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak told the yogis: let wisdom be your meal, and compassion the one who serves it. Jesus, hungry in the desert, said: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." And when the crowds who came to hear him were hungry, he didn't only teach them. He fed them.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, wisdom is the meal and the One's note already sounds in every heart. For Catholics, the deepest food is Christ himself, the bread of life, received in the Eucharist.
neighbors.shared: the best food is handed over with a kind hand.

neighbors.heading: never eat without sharing
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said wisdom is the meal, and compassion holds the ladle. The Buddha set wisdom and giving side by side too. He said that if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last mouthful, if someone were there to receive it.
neighbors.difference: Guru Nanak names a Giver and hears the One's note in every heart. The Buddha speaks of giving as training the heart to let go, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: wisdom tastes best when someone is kind enough to share it.

items.lessonTitle: Pauri 33, meaning: no power of our own

neighbors.heading: not by my own hand
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: no power to speak or keep silent, to live or die; the power is in the One's hand. Moses warns the people that once life is comfortable, they mustn't say in their hearts: "My power and the might of my hand hath gotten me this wealth." Remember instead, he says, it is God who gives the power to get it.
neighbors.difference: The Japji lands on equality: by themselves, no one is high or low. Deuteronomy speaks to Israel about its covenant and its land, reminding the people to keep God's commandments when life is good.
neighbors.shared: work hard, and stay humble about where the strength came from.

neighbors.heading: what's in your hands
neighbors.text: Today the Japji listed what isn't in our power, down to life and death. The Stoic teacher Epictetus, once a slave, opened his handbook the same way: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." Not in our power, he says: the body, property, reputation. Peace begins when you stop grabbing at those.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps one thing for us: our own judgments, desires and choices. The Japji goes further, saying even awareness and reflection aren't ours to command; the One holds the power, and acts.
neighbors.shared: letting go of what you can't hold leaves your hands free.

items.lessonTitle: The final salok: air, water, earth

neighbors.heading: from earth and water
neighbors.text: Today the Japji closed with a family: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. The Qur'an speaks of earth and water too. Of the earth: "Thereof We created you, and thereunto We return you, and thence We bring you forth a second time." And of water: "We made every living thing of water."
neighbors.difference: The salok calls earth a mother and air a Guru, a family picture of creation. In the Qur'an, earth and water are signs of Allah, made by Him and serving Him, and never called parent or guide.
neighbors.shared: the ground under you and the water you drink are gifts.

neighbors.heading: earth is my mother
neighbors.text: Today the Japji called the earth the great mother. A long hymn to the Earth in the Atharva Veda says it in Sanskrit words still quoted today: mata bhumih, putro aham prithivyah. The earth is my mother; I am her child. Some Hindu families say a morning verse asking her pardon before their feet touch the ground.
neighbors.difference: In the hymn, Earth is Prithvi, honored as a goddess with her own praises. In Gurbani, earth as mother is a picture of creation's care; Sikhs worship only the One Creator, not the earth itself.
neighbors.shared: the earth that holds you up deserves a little tenderness back.
neighbors.sources: Atharva Veda 12.1.12, the hymn to the Earth (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Haumai: the disease with its own cure

neighbors.heading: the trouble with "mine"
neighbors.text: Today the Granth called haumai, I-me, a chronic disease with its cure inside. The Buddha also saw trouble in I and mine. The Dhammapada says: "'These sons belong to me, and this wealth belongs to me,' with such thoughts a fool is tormented. He himself does not belong to himself; how much less sons and wealth?"
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the cure is turning the I toward the One, by grace and the Guru's word. The Buddha teaches anatta, not-self: look closely and no lasting I is found, with no Creator in the picture.
neighbors.shared: life gets lighter when it stops being all about me.

neighbors.heading: he must increase
neighbors.text: Today the Granth said haumai, the I-me, is a long illness, and its cure lives inside it too. Christians know that turn. John the Baptist, watching people leave him for Jesus, said: "He must increase, but I must decrease." And Paul wrote: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me."
neighbors.difference: In the Granth, the I turns toward the One through the Name and the Guru's word. For Christians, the old self is healed through Christ, who died and rose, and the new life is Christ living in the believer.
neighbors.shared: there's freedom in not having to be the center.

neighbors.heading: name it to tame it
neighbors.text: Today the Granth said the first step with the five thieves is to know them: their faces, their habits. Psychology found something close. In brain-scan studies led by Matthew Lieberman, when people put a feeling into a word, like angry or afraid, the brain's alarm center calmed more than when they just looked. Naming a feeling loosens its grip.
neighbors.difference: The Granth calls them thieves who steal the nectar of the Name, and the guard is the Name and the Guru. The psychology names no enemy and no God; it only shows that labeling a feeling quiets it.
neighbors.shared: a feeling you can name is easier to live with.
neighbors.sources: Lieberman et al., "Putting Feelings Into Words," Psychological Science (2007) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the capital sins
neighbors.text: Today the Granth named five thieves living inside: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride. Catholics keep a list too: the seven capital sins, pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony and sloth. The Church calls them capital because they're heads: other sins spring from them. And vices, it teaches, can be sorted by the virtues they oppose.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, the five begin as natural energies that become thieves when they take over, and the Name guards the house. For Catholics, sin turns a person from God, and grace heals it, especially in confession.
neighbors.shared: knowing your own weak spots is the start of being free.

items.lessonTitle: Ask about the light, not the caste

neighbors.heading: an equal eye
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said: recognize the light, don't ask about caste. The Gita has a line still quoted on this. The wise, Krishna says, look with an equal eye on a learned Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. And near the end: the Lord dwells in the heart of every being.
neighbors.difference: In the Gita, the equal eye belongs to the wise, and Hindu texts also describe varna, social orders that Hindus read in very different ways. The Gurus set caste aside in practice: one langar, one bowl of amrit.
neighbors.shared: the light in someone matters more than the label on them.

neighbors.heading: one father for all
neighbors.text: Today Guru Nanak said: recognize the light, don't ask about caste. The prophet Malachi asks: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us?" And the Mishnah explains why God began with just one person: so that no one could ever say to another, my father is greater than yours.
neighbors.difference: Judaism keeps some lines of descent, like the kohanim, the priestly families, with roles in blessing and ritual. The Gurus set birth-groups aside and gave every Khalsa Sikh one name: Singh or Kaur.
neighbors.shared: nobody's family tree is taller than anyone else's.

neighbors.heading: the other cheek
neighbors.text: Today Sheikh Farid said: if someone strikes you, don't strike back; go home in peace. Jesus said: "whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." And Paul wrote to the church in Rome: "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs hold Farid's go home beside Kabir's warrior who defends the helpless. Christians read Jesus' words in different ways too: some as a call to refuse all violence, others as a word about personal revenge.
neighbors.shared: the fight ends sooner when you don't carry it home.

neighbors.heading: repel it with better
neighbors.text: Today Sheikh Farid, a Muslim Sufi whose verses sit in the Guru Granth Sahib, said: don't strike back. His own scripture says: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend."
neighbors.difference: Here the doors overlap: Farid is a Muslim voice inside the Sikh scripture. Muslims read his kind of mercy beside the Qur'an and the Prophet's example; Sikhs sing his verses as gurbani, beside the Gurus' own hymns.
neighbors.shared: kindness can turn an enemy into a friend.

neighbors.heading: a rule for living
neighbors.text: Today rehat meant a way of living, not a checklist to earn God's favor. Catholic monks and nuns live by a rule too. Saint Benedict wrote his Rule as a school for the Lord's service, hoping to set down nothing harsh or burdensome. Prayer, work, meals and sleep all get a shape, so the whole day can turn toward God.
neighbors.difference: The Rehat Maryada is for every Sikh, kept in different degrees, at home and at work. Benedict's Rule is for monks and nuns who take vows in a monastery; other Catholics keep the Church's own precepts.
neighbors.shared: a good rule is a shape for love, not a cage.

neighbors.heading: a training you take on
neighbors.text: Today rehat meant a way of living that turns teaching into habit. Buddhists keep five precepts, and their wording is worth noticing. Each begins: I undertake the training rule to abstain from... then taking life, taking what isn't given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and intoxicants. Not a command from above. A training you take on yourself.
neighbors.difference: Rehat flows from the Guru's teaching and, for those who take amrit, comes with the five Ks. Buddhist precepts are taken on by the person, with no Creator giving them; the Buddha taught them as training, not as divine law.
neighbors.shared: a good way of living is practiced, not just believed.
neighbors.sources: The five precepts (pancasila), as chanted in Pali (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a sign upon thy hand
neighbors.text: Today the kara sat on the wrist, asking: what are these hands doing? Jews know a sign on the arm. The Shema says: "And thou shalt bind them for a sign upon thy hand, and they shall be for frontlets between thine eyes." On weekday mornings, observant Jews wind tefillin, small leather boxes holding these words, on the arm and head.
neighbors.difference: The kara is worn all day, plain steel, a circle for the One without end. Tefillin are put on for weekday morning prayer, and hold handwritten verses of the Torah inside.
neighbors.shared: what you wear on your arm can remind your hands who they serve.

neighbors.heading: a cue on your wrist
neighbors.text: Today the kara caught the light every time the hand moved. Psychology has a name for that: a cue. In Peter Gollwitzer's research on if-then plans, people who tied a goal to a concrete cue, if I see this, then I'll do that, followed through more often than people with good intentions alone. A reminder you can see helps.
neighbors.difference: The kara is an article of faith, a circle for the endless One and a bond with the Guru. A cue in psychology is a tool anyone can choose, for any goal, sacred or ordinary.
neighbors.shared: a small reminder can keep a big promise.

neighbors.heading: begin not hostilities
neighbors.text: Today dharam yudh meant a fight with limits, and Bhai Ghanaiya gave water to every wounded man. The Qur'an sets a limit too: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." Early tradition adds: don't kill women, children or the old, and don't cut down fruit trees.
neighbors.difference: Sikh rules of righteous war come mostly from tradition and history, not from one list in scripture. In Islam, the limits rest on the Qur'an and hadith, and scholars built them into a detailed body of law.
neighbors.shared: even in a fight, the other person never stops being a person.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 2:190 (Pickthall 1930) · Abu Bakr's instructions to his army, in the Muwatta of Malik, Book of Jihad (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: rules at Kurukshetra
neighbors.text: Today dharam yudh meant a fight with limits. The Mahabharata tells of rules agreed before its great war at Kurukshetra: fight only an equal; don't strike someone who is fleeing, who has surrendered, or who has no weapon; don't harm drummers or those carrying supplies. And it is honest: in the story the rules are broken, and grief follows.
neighbors.difference: The Mahabharata sets righteous war inside the dharma of the warrior class. Sikh tradition opens the saint-soldier's path to anyone who takes amrit, whatever their birth, and its rules come from the Gurus' tradition.
neighbors.shared: how you fight says as much as why you fight.

neighbors.heading: the greatest conqueror
neighbors.text: Today the Japji said: conquer your own mind, and you've conquered the world. The Dhammapada says it in battle words: "If one man conquer in battle a thousand times thousand men, and if another conquer himself, he is the greatest of conquerors." In Buddhist teaching, the real enemies are inside: greed, hatred and delusion.
neighbors.difference: Sikhs fight the five thieves with the Name, the sangat and the Guru's grace, beside the saint-soldier's duty to defend. The Buddha's way is training the mind, with no Creator to call on; the victory is freedom from craving.
neighbors.shared: the hardest win, and the best one, is over yourself.

neighbors.heading: the good that I would
neighbors.text: Today the Japji named the real battle: inside, against anger, greed and pride. Paul knew it well. "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." Then he cries out for rescue, and answers himself: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."
neighbors.difference: Sikhs fight the five thieves day by day, with the Name, the sangat and the Guru's grace. For Paul, the rescue comes through Christ's death and rising, and through the Spirit living in the believer.
neighbors.shared: you're not the only one fighting yourself, and that's a comfort.

items.lessonTitle: The Dal Khalsa and the council

neighbors.heading: good to the Holy Ghost and to us
neighbors.text: Today Sikhs gathered before the Guru Granth Sahib to decide together, and the decision became the Guru's. The early Church did something close. When the apostles and elders met in Jerusalem over a hard question, they talked it through, then wrote: "For it hath seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us." Catholics still gather bishops in councils.
neighbors.difference: A gurmata is made by the whole assembly in the Guru's presence and sealed with Ardas. In the Catholic Church, councils gather the bishops with the Pope, and Catholics believe the Holy Spirit guides their teaching.
neighbors.shared: decide together, in front of what you all respect.

neighbors.heading: the potluck of minds
neighbors.text: Today a gurmata held because the whole assembly agreed. The philosopher Aristotle argued for something similar. Many people, each with a piece of good sense, can judge better together than a few of the best alone, he wrote, the way a feast where many bring a dish beats a dinner paid for out of one purse.
neighbors.difference: A gurmata's weight comes from the Guru's presence and the prayer that seals it. Aristotle's case is about human judgment alone: pooled good sense, with no sacred presence needed.
neighbors.shared: the whole table usually sees more than one chair.

neighbors.heading: holding fast to truth
neighbors.text: Today Sikh volunteers at Guru ka Bagh were beaten and didn't strike back, and Gandhi cheered their earlier win. Gandhi called his own way satyagraha, holding fast to truth, and rooted it in ahimsa, non-harm. The Yoga Sutras say that when someone is firmly grounded in non-harm, hostility falls away in their presence.
neighbors.difference: Gandhi held non-violence as a creed for nearly every situation. The Akalis took a vow of non-violence for their campaign, and Sikh teaching also keeps the sword as a last resort to defend the helpless.
neighbors.shared: standing firm without striking back takes deep courage.
neighbors.sources: Yoga Sutras 2.35 (paraphrase) · M. K. Gandhi, Hind Swaraj (1909), on satyagraha (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the midwives said no
neighbors.text: Today Sikh volunteers held firm without violence until the gurdwaras came home. The Torah's first story of refusal is quiet too. Pharaoh ordered two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah, to kill the Hebrew baby boys. "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men-children alive." No weapons. Just a firm no.
neighbors.difference: The Akali bands protested in public, in great numbers, under a vow of non-violence. The midwives' refusal was quiet and personal, and Jewish law also permits self-defense; non-violence isn't made a rule for every case.
neighbors.shared: a firm, peaceful no can be stronger than a fist.

neighbors.heading: cast down, not destroyed
neighbors.text: Today chardi kala meant grief and getting up at the same time, again and again. Paul, beaten and on the move, wrote: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." Not pretending it's fine. Getting up anyway.
neighbors.difference: Chardi kala rises through the Name and the will of the One, asked for in every Ardas. Paul's hope rests on Jesus' death and rising: he carries Christ's dying, he says, so Christ's life can show too.
neighbors.shared: knocked down isn't the same as finished.

neighbors.heading: with hardship, ease
neighbors.text: Today families who lost everything in 1947 started over with rising spirits. The Qur'an speaks to a heavy heart: "But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." Said twice, so it sinks in. And the Islamic calendar counts from a fresh start: the Hijra, when the Prophet and his companions left Mecca for Medina.
neighbors.difference: Chardi kala is a spirit Sikhs ask for in every Ardas, through the Name. In the Qur'an, the promise of ease comes from Allah, and Muslims meet hardship with sabr, patient trust in Him.
neighbors.shared: the hard part isn't the whole story.

neighbors.heading: the labor of their hands
neighbors.text: Today Sikh men milled lumber far from home, living kirat karni, honest work with their own hands. Catholics honor work too. Saint Benedict wrote that idleness is the enemy of the soul, and that monks are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands. And the Gospels remember Jesus as the carpenter's son.
neighbors.difference: Kirat karni sits beside remembering the Name and sharing what you earn. For Benedict, work is woven between set hours of prayer in a monastery, and the Church teaches that work shares in God's own creating.
neighbors.shared: honest work, done well, has its own quiet holiness.
neighbors.sources: Rule of Saint Benedict, ch. 48 (paraphrase) · Matthew 13:55 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: right livelihood
neighbors.text: Today Sikh men milled lumber in Canada, living kirat karni, an honest living by their own work. The Buddha put work on his path too. Right livelihood is one step of the Eightfold Path, and he named five trades to avoid: trading in weapons, in people, in meat, in intoxicants and in poisons.
neighbors.difference: For Sikhs, honest work goes with remembering the One and sharing with others. In the Buddha's teaching, right livelihood means earning without causing harm, as training on the path to freedom, with no Creator involved.
neighbors.shared: how you earn your bread is part of who you are.

neighbors.heading: bread to the hungry
neighbors.text: Today the langar traveled, from Amritsar's kitchen to floods and borders. Jews hear a prophet's call. Isaiah says the fast God wants is this: "Is it not to deal thy bread to the hungry, and that thou bring the poor that are cast out to thy house?" And early in the Passover seder comes an invitation: let all who are hungry come and eat.
neighbors.difference: Langar is a free kitchen at the gurdwara, open to all, everyone on the same floor. Jewish giving is tzedakah, a commanded duty of justice, and the seder's invitation is spoken at a family table at Passover.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person is a guest, not a stranger.
neighbors.sources: Isaiah 58:7 (JPS 1917) · Passover Haggadah, Ha Lachma Anya (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: giving feeds the giver
neighbors.text: Today the langar went out to floods and borders. Psychologists have measured part of why that feels right. In a study led by Elizabeth Dunn, people were handed money to spend by evening. Those told to spend it on someone else ended the day happier than those told to spend it on themselves. Giving fed the giver too.
neighbors.difference: Langar is seva, service offered to the Guru, seeing the one light in everyone. The study names no God and no duty; it only shows giving lifts the giver's mood, which Sikhs wouldn't call the reason.
neighbors.shared: feeding someone else has a way of filling you up.
neighbors.sources: Dunn, Aknin & Norton, "Spending Money on Others Promotes Happiness," Science (2008) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: that ye may know one another
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: no one is my enemy, and no one is a stranger. The Qur'an speaks to all people: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Different peoples aren't made to stay strangers. They're made to get to know each other.
neighbors.difference: Guru Arjan finds no stranger because the one God is present in everyone, seen in holy company. The Qur'an speaks of Allah as Creator of all, distinct from creation, and honors people by their conduct, not their tribe.
neighbors.shared: a stranger is just someone you haven't met yet.

neighbors.heading: the earth is one family
neighbors.text: Today Guru Arjan sang: no one is a stranger. A Sanskrit verse from the Maha Upanishad says it this way: counting "this one is mine, that one is a stranger" is for small minds. For the large-hearted, vasudhaiva kutumbakam: the whole earth is one family.
neighbors.difference: The verse grounds it in a large heart, and some Hindu schools add that one Self lives in all. Guru Arjan's reason is the one God present in everyone, seen in holy company, not that each person is God.
neighbors.shared: the whole earth can feel like one big family table.

neighbors.heading: may all beings be happy
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas ended with sarbat da bhala: the good of all, even those who did the hurting. Buddhists chant a wish just as wide. The Metta Sutta asks that all beings be happy and at ease: the weak and the strong, the seen and unseen, near and far, born and yet to be born, loved the way a mother guards her only child.
neighbors.difference: The Ardas asks the One for everyone's good, by your will, leaving its shape to the Giver. Metta is a wish grown in the heart, addressed to no Creator; the practice changes the one who wishes.
neighbors.shared: the best wishes are the ones with no one left out.

neighbors.heading: pray for them
neighbors.text: Today the Ardas asked for the good of all, including those who did the hurting. Jesus asked the same of his followers: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you."
neighbors.difference: Sarbat da bhala grows from seeing the one light in every person. Christians pray for enemies following Jesus, who, the Gospel says, prayed on the cross for the ones crucifying him.
neighbors.shared: the widest prayer leaves no one out, not even the one who hurt you.
